SYDNEY, Oct 12 : Asian share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday as earnings season loomed as a challenge to sky-high tech valuations, while oil was choppy after strikes on shipping and airports in the Gulf. There was considerable confusion about President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, which neither side had confirmed. Trump's proposal for Russia to increase its exports of diesel was also under fire from Republican and Democratic senators as potentially illegal. Brent futures started higher but soon slipped 1.1 per cent to $103.50 a barrel, away from the recent top of $109.97, while US crude futures lost 1.2 per cent to $90.73 a barrel.

South Korean stocks fell 1.1 per cent, while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was little changed. On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures edged up 0.2 per cent, while Nasdaq futures firmed 0.5 per cent. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.4 per cent, while DAX futures gained 0.4 per cent and FTSE futures added 0.3 per cent. Trade was thin with Japan markets shut and the US on a partial holiday ahead of the earnings season with major US banks kicking off on Tuesday. S&P 500 earnings are expected to have jumped by more than 30 per cent in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, though the bulk of that comes from the tech sector. My Bui, an economist at AMP, noted all the gains in the S&P 500 since mid-September had been in tech, while investors were demanding higher yields to fund the massive borrowing for AI. The US investment-grade credit default swap index, which tracks the cost of insurance against default, had also risen sharply to its highest level since the Iran war began. "Overall, wider spreads suggest investors are questioning whether AI revenues can keep pace with rising borrowing costs," added Bui. "Corporate bond issuance to fund AI capex, combined with wider high-yield spreads, will raise refinancing costs as the current wave of debt matures over the next few years." US CPI TO HEAT UP, BUT CORE COOLER The flood of corporate debt has added to pressure in sovereign markets, driving Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week and lifting the discount applied to company earnings. The market faces fresh challenges this week from US data on consumer and producer prices and retail sales. Rising energy costs are expected to lift CPI by a hefty 0.6 per cent to an annual 3.7 per cent, though the core is seen cooler at 0.2 per cent and 2.5 per cent. "Oil prices remain higher than we had assumed as shipping costs have soared, and product prices are even higher," said Bruce Kasman, head of global economics at JPMorgan. "The signals on inflation point to a sharp rebound in headline inflation that will squeeze purchasing power and a firming in core inflation that will keep central banks focused on near-term hikes." Markets imply only an 18 per cent chance of a rate rise from the Federal Reserve this month, but an 85 per cent chance of a hike in December. Investors are also wagering on hikes in the EU, Japan and UK before year end. In currency markets, the euro remained on the defensive at $1.1201 having fallen for five weeks straight amid concerns about government deficits in Europe. The dollar index held near 17-month highs at 102.25, but has stalled on the yen at 158.15 as the threat of Japanese intervention deters speculators for now. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold rose 0.3 per cent to $4,206 an ounce, having managed to bounce more than 1 per cent last week.

Source: Reuters

(Corrects to drop byline with no text changes) By Courtney Rozen WASHINGTON, Oct 11 : American AI developers can give the British government early access to AI models for safety testing without running afoul of US President Donald Trump's administration, the Telegraph newspaper said on Sunday. The Trump administration has reversed a decision that requested developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic not to share new AI models with Britain's AI Security Institute before release, the newspaper said.

The change signals a softer stance by the Trump administration on international AI safety efforts, giving US developers greater latitude to cooperate with Britain as policymakers grapple with how to oversee the increasingly powerful technology. Spokespersons for Trump, OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters. Britain's AI Security Institute, set up after the world's first AI safety summit in 2023, tests the most advanced AI models to evaluate their capabilities and the risk of misuse.  Trump has repeatedly dismissed calls for binding safety requirements on AI developers, a position that appears to be shifting. His newly launched AI task force said on Friday developers must report security incidents with their AI models.

Source: Reuters

Oct 11 : Amazon is in talks to acquire artificial intelligence startup Decart in a deal that could be valued at around $7 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. • Decart's Lucy model, backed by Nvidia, can edit live video in real time, according to the company's website. It has also developed Oasis, a model that generates simulated environments to train and test robotics and autonomous-driving systems. • Decart was valued at nearly $4 billion in May, the Journal report said, citing PitchBook data. • Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Decart and Amazon did not respond to requests for comment.

MOSCOW, Oct 11 : Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Sunday that its infrastructure had been damaged in a drone attack, resulting in the complete shutdown of its data centre in the Vladimir region. No one was injured in the attack, but some of Yandex's services are currently unavailable to users, the company said. This is the third major data centre to have been taken out of action in the last few days. On Friday, Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia's AI development and is sometimes called "Russia's Google", said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action. A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down Yandex's data hub in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model are housed.

Source: Reuters

FAST

BENGALURU, Oct 11 : Elon Musk said he would price Starlink's satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Mukesh Ambani's low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival billionaire days before Jio's parent launches India's largest-ever IPO. Jio Platforms, which owns the telecom arm, is targeting a valuation of $106 billion in the offering. Much like SpaceX-owned Starlink, Jio's own satellite venture is also awaiting final security clearance to launch. Cheap data is the playbook that built Jio in India, and the one Musk has used in markets like Kenya to unsettle local telecom players. SpaceX now plans to enter the mobile carrier market itself, starting in the US. Musk did not specify prices for India, where mobile data costs about 8 cents per gigabyte, among the lowest in the world.

"Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable," he said in a post on his social media platform X on Saturday. "The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani's profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business," Musk added. 'PRIME MINISTER AMBANI' The billionaire's remarks were the latest in a series of X posts where he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government and Ambani of stalling Starlink's entry into one of the world's biggest internet markets to favour market leader Jio. The posts have marked a sharp turn for Musk, who has long enjoyed a warm public rapport with Modi. India's government has denied any bias in its approval process, noting that the three satellite ventures seeking to launch, including Starlink's and Jio's, are all awaiting final security clearance. Late on Friday, Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as "Prime Minister Ambani" and asking whether he would "consider allowing Starlink to compete". Reliance has not responded to requests for comment on Musk's remarks.

Source: Reuters

Oct 10 : Nvidia is in talks to deepen its investment in open-source startup Reflection AI or acquire it, the Financial Times reported on Saturday, citing people with direct knowledge of the matter. • Talks are at an early stage and a deal could take several forms, including a so-called acqui-hire arrangement where Nvidia would hire staff and license technology rather than pursue a full acquisition, potentially avoiding a lengthy regulatory review, the newspaper said. • An agreement could be reached in the coming weeks, according to the report, which cited multiple people familiar with the matter, while adding that the discussions could still fall apart. • Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Nvidia and Reflection did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside of regular business hours.

• Nvidia is already a major financial backer and strategic investor in Reflection AI, having invested $800 million in the startup, the FT reported. • Founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, Reflection develops tools that automate software development, a fast-growing use case for AI. • Reflection's chief executive, Laskin, told CNBC in April that the Nvidia-backed startup was raising fresh capital at a pre-money valuation of $25 billion. • The company on Monday launched its first open-weight model, Beam, as it seeks to compete in coding and agentic tasks with lower-cost Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Kimi.
